requirements.requirement: inventory-api runs as a managed systemd service on node1
requirements.summary: A systemd unit (inventory-api.service) was created with Restart=always, enabled and started; systemctl is-active confirmed 'active' and /health and /inventory responded correctly.

requirements.requirement: A healthy baseline is established before inducing disruption
requirements.summary: Pre-disruption baseline captured free memory, service active state, and successful /health and /inventory responses with seeded data.

requirements.requirement: A memory-hungry process drives the system out of memory and is the process the kernel OOM-killer stops (not inventory-api)
requirements.summary: mem-hog (default oom_score_adj=0) was started and allowed to consume memory; free memory collapsed then recovered as mem-hog's service state flipped to failed; dmesg directly shows the kernel oom-killer selecting and killing PID 1438 (python3, mem-hog.service, oom_score_adj=0). inventory-api's PID (1335, oom_score_adj=-1000) was never targeted.

requirements.requirement: inventory-api keeps serving throughout and after the OOM event
requirements.summary: Post-OOM check shows inventory-api active with the same unchanged PID (1335), /health returning ok, and both GET and POST /inventory succeeding, including persistence of a new write made after the kill event.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are directly demonstrated: inventory-api runs as an enabled, restart-always systemd service with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000; a deliberately unprotected memory-hog process drove the system out of memory and was the process the kernel OOM-killer selected and killed (confirmed via dmesg); and inventory-api continued serving reads and writes on the same PID throughout and after the event, with data intact. The independent, non-contractual node-restart evidence protocol was also completed cleanly: a pre-reboot boot_id and healthy baseline were captured, systemctl reboot was issued and acknowledged (stream disconnect consistent with reboot), the post-reboot boot_id differed as expected, and inventory-api recovered (new PID, OOM protection reapplied from the unit file, and all data including the post-OOM test row) with the mem-hog test service remaining disabled.
limitations: The task contract itself does not require reboot survival/persistence, so the restart evidence is supplemental confirmation rather than a scored material outcome, though it strengthens overall confidence.

mem-hog.service and its script were left installed but disabled/stopped rather than fully removed after the OOM test, a minor and low-risk residue directly tied to demonstrating the OOM-selection requirement.

The exec-stream disconnection during systemctl reboot (cmd-fea07eee08674e2b) is only indirectly confirmed as a genuine reboot; the changed boot_id in the subsequent commands is the primary direct evidence of an actual restart.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor's state-changing commands map cleanly to task purposes: creating the inventory-api service (required), creating and running the mem-hog test service (necessary to directly demonstrate the OOM-selection requirement), and the mandatory node-restart protocol (reboot issued and recovered cleanly, boot_id changed as expected, no residual disruption). The one attempted `semanage fcontext` command failed (binary not found) but caused no state change. Minor residue: the mem-hog.service unit file and /opt/inventory-api/memhog.py remain on disk after testing (cmd-aaaa0b8f521d48ca stopped and reset-failed it, and it was confirmed disabled so it will not run again), rather than being fully removed post-test; this is low-risk since the service is disabled/stopped and was directly required to prove the OOM-selection behavior, but it is leftover test tooling rather than fully cleaned-up state. No destructive, broad, or security-weakening mutations were observed; failed-services and listening-socket diffs across lifecycle snapshots show only the expected inventory-api listener and post-reboot PID churn.
